title: Question 4
stem:
A ball of mass $M$ is held on a horizontal surface by two identical extended springs, as illustrated in Fig. 4.1.

{{figure:figure_4_1}}

Fig. 4.1

One spring is attached to a fixed point. The other spring is attached to an oscillator.

The oscillator is switched off. The ball is displaced sideways along the axis of the springs and is then released. The variation with time $t$ of the displacement $x$ of the ball is shown in Fig. 4.2.

{{figure:figure_4_2}}

Fig. 4.2

parts.label: (a)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Think about what happens to the total energy of a real oscillator over time when friction or air resistance acts, rather than what happens to the shape of the graph.
parts.proper_answer: Damping is the loss of energy from an oscillating system due to a resistive force.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What Damping Really Means**
Think of an ideal oscillator that would go on forever with constant energy. In real life friction, air resistance or other resistive forces do negative work on the moving mass, so mechanical energy is removed as heat or sound.

Step 2: **Examiner-Standard Definition**
So damping is defined simply as loss of energy from the oscillating system. You do not need to mention amplitude here, just the energy idea: $$ \text{damping = energy removed per oscillation due to dissipative forces} $$

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text: the evidence provided by Fig. 4.2 that the motion of the ball is damped.
hints: Hint 1: Look carefully at the successive peaks in Fig. 4.2 from t = 0 to t = 2.4 s and compare the maximum values of x on each swing.
parts.proper_answer: The amplitude of oscillation decreases with time, from 1.5 cm to about 0.65 cm.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Reading Damping From the Graph**
If there were no damping, every peak would reach the same $x$ value of 1.5 cm. In Fig. 4.2 the first peak is 1.5 cm, the next positive peak near 0.8 s is about 1.15 cm, then about 0.85 cm, then about 0.65 cm. The envelope is shrinking.

Step 2: **Link to Damping**
A shrinking envelope means maximum displacement is getting smaller because energy is being lost. That steady fall in amplitude with time is the direct visual evidence for damping.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.part_stem:
The acceleration $a$ and the displacement $x$ of the ball are related by the expression

$$a = -\left(\frac{2k}{M}\right)x$$

where $k$ is the spring constant of one of the springs.

The mass $M$ of the ball is $1.2\text{ kg}$.
parts.text: Use data from Fig. 4.2 to determine the angular frequency $\omega$ of the oscillations of the ball.
hints: Hint 1: Find the time for one full oscillation from Fig. 4.2, for example from the start at t = 0 to the next time the curve is at a maximum moving the same way.
Hint 2: Recall how angular frequency $\omega$ is linked to period $T$ for SHM and check the unit $\text{rad s}^{-1}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Get the Period T From Fig. 4.2**
You are sitting with the graph. Start at the maximum at $t = 0$. The next maximum in the same direction is at $t = 0.80\text{ s}$. You can also use zero crossings or minima, for example minima at 0.40 s and 1.20 s give $T = 0.80\text{ s}$. Damping is light so $T$ is almost constant.

Step 2: **Convert Period to Angular Frequency**
For SHM: $$ \omega = \frac{2\pi}{T} $$ Substitute: $$ \omega = \frac{2\pi}{0.80} \approx 7.85 \approx 7.9\text{ rad s}^{-1} $$ Keep 2 significant figures to match the data.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: Use your answer in (i) to determine the value of $k$.
hints: Hint 1: Compare the given $a = -(2k/M)x$ with the standard SHM form $a = -\omega^2 x$ to see what $\omega^2$ must equal.
Hint 2: Rearrange that relation to make $k$ the subject and substitute $M = 1.2\text{ kg}$ and your $\omega$ from (b)(i).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Identify omega in Terms of k and M**
Standard SHM is: $$ a = -\omega^2 x $$ You are given: $$ a = -\left(\frac{2k}{M}\right)x $$ The factor 2 appears because both springs pull when the ball moves. Comparing gives: $$ \omega^2 = \frac{2k}{M} $$

Step 2: **Solve for k**
Rearrange: $$ k = \frac{M\omega^2}{2} $$ Using $M = 1.2\text{ kg}$ and $\omega = 7.9\text{ rad s}^{-1}$: $$ k = \frac{1.2 \times 7.9^2}{2} \approx 37\text{ N m}^{-1} $$

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.part_stem:
The oscillator is switched on. The amplitude of oscillation of the oscillator is constant.

The angular frequency of the oscillations is gradually increased from $0.7\omega$ to $1.3\omega$, where $\omega$ is the angular frequency calculated in (b)(i).

markscheme_points.text: (one) smooth curve, not touching the f-axis, with two conc

hints: Hint 1: Think about what happens to the ball's amplitude when the driver frequency is far from natural frequency compared to when it matches it.
Hint 2: Recall where on the frequency axis the resonance peak must occur for light damping and what shape the curve has around it.
parts.proper_answer: Smooth resonance curve starting low at 0.7$\omega$, rising to a single sharp maximum at 1.0$\omega$, then falling toward 1.3$\omega$, not touching the frequency axis.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Picture Forced Oscillation**
The oscillator now drives the ball. When driving frequency is well below or above the natural frequency $\omega$, the ball barely responds. When driving frequency equals natural frequency, energy transfer is most efficient and amplitude is maximum. This is resonance.

Step 2: **Sketch the Curve**
Draw one smooth continuous curve. It should be relatively low at $0.7\omega$, rise steadily to a clear peak exactly at $1.0\omega$, then fall again by $1.3\omega$. Keep the whole line above the axis because amplitude is never zero with a constant driver.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.text:
Some sand is now sprinkled on the horizontal surface.

The angular frequency of the oscillations is again gradually increased from $0.7\omega$ to $1.3\omega$.

State two changes that occur to the line you have drawn on Fig. 4.3.

markscheme_points.text: peak at (slightly) lower angular frequency/peak moves
markscheme_points.guidance: any two points, one mark each

hints: Hint 1: Sand on the surface adds friction, so think about whether more energy is lost per cycle and what that does to the maximum amplitude at resonance.
Hint 2: Think about how heavier damping affects the sharpness of the resonance and the exact position of the peak frequency.
parts.proper_answer: Any two from: peak amplitude is lower, resonance peak is flatter / broader / less sharp, peak occurs at slightly lower angular frequency.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **More Damping Means Less Response**
Sand increases the resistive force, so more energy is dissipated each cycle. At resonance the steady amplitude is set by energy supplied = energy lost, so the balance happens at a smaller amplitude. The whole curve is therefore lower.

Step 2: **Broader and Shifted Peak**
Heavy damping makes resonance less sharp, so the peak looks flatter and wider. The maximum also moves very slightly to a frequency below the natural frequency $\omega$. Any two of lower peak, flatter peak, shift to lower frequency earn the marks.

key_concepts: effect of increased damping on resonance
